{まい} is a classical negative volitional ('won't, not intend to'). Pairing a verb's volitional form with its {まい} form gives 'whether X happens or not': {降[ふ]ろうが降[ふ]るまいが} 'whether it rains or not'. The conclusion (unchanged) follows. {〜ようと〜まいと} is a variant with the same meaning.

{まい} forms: Group 1 — dictionary form + {まい} ({行[い]くまい}); Group 2 — {食[た]べまい} or {食[た]べるまい}; {する} → {するまい／しまい／すまい}; {来[く]る} → {来[く]るまい／来[こ]まい}.

**Register:** fairly formal but used in emphatic speech too ({信[しん]じようが信[しん]じまいが}). A stronger version of {〜ても〜なくても}.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ろうが降[ふ]るまいが、試合[しあい]は行[おこな]われる。
examples.en: Whether it rains or not, the match will go ahead.

examples.jp: 信[しん]じようが信[しん]じまいが、これは本当[ほんとう]にあった話[はなし]だ。
examples.en: Believe it or not, this really happened.

examples.jp: 君[きみ]が賛成[さんせい]しようがしまいが、私[わたし]の気持[きも]ちは変[か]わらない。
examples.en: Whether you agree or not, my feelings won't change.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]が来[こ]ようが来[く]るまいが、会議[かいぎ]は予定[よてい]どおり始[はじ]める。
examples.en: Whether he comes or not, we'll start the meeting as scheduled.

points.notes: {〜まい} alone also means 'probably not' or 'I won't': {二度[にど]と行[い]くまい} 'I'll never go again' (see Unit 14).

quiz.q: 君[きみ]が行[い]こうが行[い]く＿＿、私[わたし]は一人[ひとり]で行[い]く。
quiz.en: Whether you go or not, I'm going on my own.

quiz.q: 彼[かれ]が＿＿しまいが、私[わたし]には関係[かんけい]ない。
quiz.en: Whether he gets married or not has nothing to do with me.
choices: 結婚[けっこん]しようが

points.title: 〜(よ)うにも〜ない
points.meaning: (even if I) want to (X), I can't
points.structure: Verb volitional + にも + same verb (potential, negative)
points.explanation:
{〜(よ)うにも〜ない} means 'I'd like to do X / I try to do X, but circumstances make it impossible'. The same verb is repeated: {買[か]おうにも買[か]えない} 'I want to buy it but can't', {帰[かえ]ろうにも帰[かえ]れない} 'I want to go home but can't'.

The reason is usually stated first: no money, no trains, a fever, not knowing someone's number.

**Register:** neutral; used in conversation as well as writing. A natural, practical pattern.

examples.jp: 財布[さいふ]を忘[わす]れたので、買[か]おうにも買[か]えなかった。
examples.en: I'd forgotten my wallet, so I couldn't buy it even though I wanted to.

examples.jp: 熱[ねつ]が高[たか]くて、起[お]きようにも起[お]きられない。
examples.en: My fever is so high I can't get up, however much I try.

examples.jp: 終電[しゅうでん]が出[で]てしまい、帰[かえ]ろうにも帰[かえ]れなくなった。
examples.en: The last train had gone, so I couldn't get home.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]の連絡先[れんらくさき]が分[わ]からないので、謝[あやま]ろうにも謝[あやま]れない。
examples.en: I don't know how to contact him, so I can't apologise even though I want to.

points.notes: The second verb is in potential negative form ({〜られない}, {〜えない}). With {する}-verbs: {連絡[れんらく]しようにもできない}.

quiz.q: 電話[でんわ]番号[ばんごう]を知[し]らないので、連絡[れんらく]しよう＿＿できない。
quiz.en: I don't know her phone number, so I can't contact her even if I want to.

quiz.q: 足[あし]をけがしているので、逃[に]げようにも＿＿。
quiz.en: I've hurt my leg, so I can't run away even if I want to.

points.title: 〜ではあるまいし／〜じゃあるまいし
points.meaning: it's not as if (you're X), so ...
points.structure: Noun + ではあるまいし / じゃあるまいし
points.explanation:
{〜ではあるまいし} means 'you're not X, so (obviously)...'. It dismisses a situation as unnecessary or ridiculous by pointing out that the person isn't a child, a god, a beginner, etc. The second half is usually advice, criticism or a statement of the obvious: {子[こ]どもじゃあるまいし、一人[ひとり]で行[い]けるでしょう} 'You're not a child — you can go by yourself.'

**Register:** {じゃあるまいし} is conversational and very common in real speech — often used to tease or scold. Not for formal writing or for speaking to superiors.

examples.jp: 子[こ]どもじゃあるまいし、一人[ひとり]で病院[びょういん]ぐらい行[い]けるでしょう。
examples.en: You're not a child — you can at least go to the hospital on your own.

examples.jp: 初[はじ]めてじゃあるまいし、そんなに緊張[きんちょう]することはないよ。
examples.en: It's not your first time — no need to be so nervous.

examples.jp: 神様[かみさま]ではあるまいし、未来[みらい]のことなんて分[わ]かるはずがない。
examples.en: I'm not God — how could I possibly know the future?

examples.jp: 一生[いっしょう]会[あ]えないわけではあるまいし、そんなに泣[な]かないで。
examples.en: It's not as if we'll never see each other again, so don't cry like that.

points.notes: Similar to {〜ではないのだから}, but more emotional and dismissive.

quiz.q: 子[こ]ども＿＿、そんなことで泣[な]くなよ。
quiz.en: You're not a kid — don't cry over something like that.

quiz.q: 超能力者[ちょうのうりょくしゃ]で＿＿、人[ひと]の心[こころ]なんて読[よ]めるわけがない。
quiz.en: I'm not a psychic — there's no way I can read people's minds.

units.title: Formal written style and classical remnants
units.summary: The building blocks of serious written Japanese: the {である} style, classical negatives ({ず}, {ぬ}, {ざる}), {べし}, {ごとし}, {まい} and {んとする} — forms you'll meet every day in newspapers, essays, proverbs and literature.

points.title: である調[ちょう]
points.meaning: the formal written plain style (is / am / are)
points.structure: Noun / な-adj + である・であった・であろう・ではない・ではなかろうか / Verb・い-adj + のである・であろう
points.explanation:
Japanese has two plain styles. {だ} is used in casual speech and diaries; {である} is the plain style of **serious writing**: academic papers, newspaper editorials, essays, reports, legal texts and much literature.

Key forms:
- {〜である} / {〜であった} — is / was
- {〜であろう} — probably is (written {だろう}); also after verbs: {続[つづ]くであろう}
- {〜ではなかろうか} — isn't it perhaps... (a soft written claim)
- {〜のである} — explanatory (written {〜のだ}); very common
- {〜であり、〜} — connective 'is X, and'

Note: {である} does not attach directly to verbs or i-adjectives ({✕高[たか]いである}); use {高[たか]いのである}.

**Register:** essential for reading anything serious, and for writing reports or theses in Japan. It sounds stiff in conversation, except in speeches ({〜でありまして}).

examples.jp: 吾輩[わがはい]は猫[ねこ]である。名前[なまえ]はまだ無[な]い。
examples.en: I am a cat. As yet I have no name. (Natsume Sōseki)

examples.jp: 日本[にほん]は世界[せかい]有数[ゆうすう]の長寿国[ちょうじゅこく]である。
examples.en: Japan is one of the countries with the longest life expectancy in the world.

examples.jp: 本研究[ほんけんきゅう]の目的[もくてき]は、若者[わかもの]の消費[しょうひ]行動[こうどう]を明[あき]らかにすることである。
examples.en: The aim of this study is to clarify the consumer behaviour of young people.

examples.jp: この問題[もんだい]の解決[かいけつ]は容易[ようい]ではないであろう。
examples.en: Solving this problem will probably not be easy.

examples.jp: 教育[きょういく]こそが、国[くに]の未来[みらい]を左右[さゆう]する鍵[かぎ]ではなかろうか。
examples.en: Is it not education, above all, that holds the key to the nation's future?

points.notes: Don't mix styles: a text in {である} style shouldn't suddenly switch to {です／ます} or {だ}. When writing reports in Japan, choose one style and stick to it.

quiz.q: 健康[けんこう]は何[なに]ものにも代[か]えがたい財産[ざいさん]＿＿。
quiz.en: Health is an asset that nothing can replace.

quiz.q: この傾向[けいこう]は今後[こんご]も続[つづ]く＿＿。
quiz.en: This trend will probably continue in the future.

points.title: 〜ず／〜ずに (written negative)
points.meaning: not; without (doing)
points.structure: Verb ない-stem + ず / ずに / ず、 (する → せず, 来[く]る → 来[こ]ず)
points.explanation:
{ず} is the classical negative, still alive in modern Japanese:

- **{〜ずに}** — 'without doing' = {〜ないで}. Common in both writing and speech: {何[なに]も言[い]わずに出[で]て行[い]った}.
- **{〜ず、}** — 'not X, and...' as a connector in writing = {〜なくて}: {原因[げんいん]は分[わ]からず、調査[ちょうさ]が続[つづ]いている}.
- **Sentence-final {ず}** — in **news headlines**: {首相[しゅしょう]、会見[かいけん]に応[おう]じず} 'PM refuses press conference'.
- **Fixed phrases**: {知[し]らず知[し]らず} (without realising), {相変[あいか]わらず} (as usual), {思[おも]わず} (involuntarily), {少[すく]なからず} (not a little).

Remember: {する} → {せず}, not {✕しず}.

**Register:** {〜ずに} and the fixed phrases are everyday Japanese; the others are written.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]も言[い]わずに部屋[へや]を出[で]て行[い]った。
examples.en: He left the room without saying anything.

examples.jp: 知[し]らず知[し]らずのうちに、日本語[にほんご]で考[かんが]えるようになっていた。
examples.en: Before I knew it, I had started thinking in Japanese.

examples.jp: 原因[げんいん]は今[いま]も分[わ]からず、調査[ちょうさ]が続[つづ]いている。
examples.en: The cause is still unknown, and the investigation continues.

examples.jp: 首相[しゅしょう]、記者[きしゃ]会見[かいけん]に応[おう]じず
examples.en: (Headline) PM declines to hold press conference

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]にも負[ま]けず、風[かぜ]にも負[ま]けず。
examples.en: Not losing to the rain, not losing to the wind. (Miyazawa Kenji)

points.notes: Many N1 patterns are built on {ず}: {ずじまい}, {ずにはおかない}, {ずにはすまない}, {ずとも} 'even without'.

quiz.q: 彼[かれ]は朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]も食[た]べ＿＿、急[いそ]いで家[いえ]を出[で]た。
quiz.en: He rushed out of the house without even eating breakfast.

quiz.q: 彼女[かのじょ]は誰[だれ]にも相談[そうだん]＿＿、留学[りゅうがく]を決[き]めた。
quiz.en: She decided to study abroad without consulting anyone.

points.title: 〜ぬ／〜ざる (classical negatives before nouns)
points.meaning: not (in fixed phrases and noun modifiers)
points.structure: Verb ない-stem + ぬ (+ Noun) / Verb ない-stem + ざる + Noun / ざるを得[え]ない (する → せぬ／せざる)
points.explanation:
Two more classical negatives survive mainly in fixed expressions:

**{ぬ}** — a negative that can end a sentence or modify a noun. Found in set phrases: {見知[みし]らぬ人[ひと]} (a stranger), {思[おも]わぬ} (unexpected), {言[い]わぬが花[はな]} (some things are better left unsaid), {せぬ} (written 'does not'). In speech, its descendant {ん} lives on in {すみません}, {知[し]らん} (Kansai/older men), {分[わ]からん}.

**{ざる}** — used only before nouns: {知[し]られざる} 'little-known', {見[み]えざる} 'invisible', {欠[か]くべからざる}. Also the very common N2 pattern {〜ざるを得[え]ない} 'have no choice but to'.

**Register:** literary, but many set phrases are everyday Japanese. {知[し]られざる} is a favourite in documentary and book titles.

examples.jp: 見知[みし]らぬ人[ひと]から突然[とつぜん]声[こえ]をかけられた。
examples.en: A stranger suddenly spoke to me.

examples.jp: 思[おも]わぬところで、昔[むかし]の恩師[おんし]に再会[さいかい]した。
examples.en: I ran into my old teacher in the most unexpected place.

examples.jp: 知[し]られざる歴史[れきし]の真実[しんじつ]に迫[せま]るドキュメンタリーだ。
examples.en: It's a documentary that explores little-known historical truths.

examples.jp: 経営[けいえい]が悪化[あっか]し、人員[じんいん]削減[さくげん]に踏[ふ]み切[き]らざるを得[え]なかった。
examples.en: As the business deteriorated, we had no choice but to cut staff.

points.notes: Don't confuse classical negative {ぬ} with the completion {ぬ} in old poetry ({風[かぜ]立[た]ちぬ} 'the wind has risen'). Context and grammar differ, and the second is rare outside literature and titles.

quiz.q: ＿＿人[ひと]について行[い]ってはいけないよ。
quiz.en: You mustn't go off with strangers.

quiz.q: 会社[かいしゃ]の方針[ほうしん]なので、従[したが]わ＿＿を得[え]ない。
quiz.en: It's company policy, so I have no choice but to follow it.

points.title: 〜べし／〜べき
points.meaning: must; should; (べき + noun) that ought to / remarkable
points.structure: Verb (dictionary form) + べし (sentence end) / べき + Noun (する → すべし／すべき)
points.explanation:
{べし} is the classical 'should / must'. Its forms are spread across modern Japanese:

- **{べし}** (sentence end) — a strong command or rule, in old-style regulations, mottos and slogans: {期限[きげん]までに提出[ていしゅつ]すべし}. Online, {〜恐[おそ]るべし} is used jokingly: 'X is formidable!'.
- **{べき}** (before nouns) — 'that should be': {驚[おどろ]くべきこと} 'an astonishing thing', {恐[おそ]るべき速[はや]さ} 'terrifying speed'. (You know {〜べきだ} from N2.)
- **{べく}** — 'in order to' (Unit 11).
- **{べからず}** — 'must not' (Unit 13).

**Register:** {べし} is classical and emphatic; {べき} is everyday written Japanese.

examples.jp: 書類[しょるい]は期限[きげん]までに提出[ていしゅつ]すべし。
examples.en: Documents must be submitted by the deadline.

examples.jp: 運動[うんどう]の前[まえ]には、必[かなら]ず準備[じゅんび]運動[うんどう]をすべし。
examples.en: Always warm up before exercising.

examples.jp: 驚[おどろ]くべきことに、彼[かれ]はたった一年[いちねん]で日本語[にほんご]を習得[しゅうとく]した。
examples.en: Astonishingly, he mastered Japanese in just one year.

examples.jp: 恐[おそ]るべき速[はや]さで、ウイルスは世界中[せかいじゅう]に広[ひろ]がった。
examples.en: The virus spread around the world at a frightening speed.

points.notes: {恐[おそ]る} is the classical form of {恐[おそ]れる}; it survives in {恐[おそ]るべき} and {恐[おそ]るべし}.

quiz.q: 集合[しゅうごう]時間[じかん]は厳守[げんしゅ]す＿＿。
quiz.en: The meeting time must be strictly observed.

quiz.q: 驚[おどろ]く＿＿ことに、その小説[しょうせつ]を書[か]いたのは十二歳[じゅうにさい]の少女[しょうじょ]だった。
quiz.en: Astonishingly, the novel was written by a twelve-year-old girl.

points.title: 〜ごとし／〜ごとく／〜ごとき
points.meaning: like; as; as if
points.structure: Noun + の + ごとし / ごとく (+ Verb) / ごとき (+ Noun); Verb + (が)ごとし
points.explanation:
{ごとし} is the classical equivalent of {ようだ} 'like, as if'. It conjugates just like {ようだ}:

- {〜のごとし} = {〜のようだ} (sentence end)
- {〜のごとく} = {〜のように} (+ verb or adjective)
- {〜のごとき} = {〜のような} (+ noun)

You'll meet it in proverbs ({光陰[こういん]矢[や]のごとし} 'time flies like an arrow'), literature, formal writing ({前述[ぜんじゅつ]のごとく} 'as stated above') and speeches.

**Register:** literary/classical. In modern writing, {〜のごとく} and {〜かのごとく} ('as if') are fairly common; {ごとし} at the end of a sentence is mostly in proverbs. (For {私[わたし]ごとき} 'the likes of me', see Unit 7.)

examples.jp: 光陰[こういん]矢[や]のごとし。
examples.en: Time flies like an arrow.

examples.jp: 過[す]ぎたるはなお及[およ]ばざるがごとし。
examples.en: Too much is as bad as too little.

examples.jp: 前述[ぜんじゅつ]のごとく、この計画[けいかく]には多[おお]くの問題[もんだい]がある。
examples.en: As stated above, this plan has many problems.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は水[みず]を得[え]た魚[さかな]のごとく、生[い]き生[い]きと働[はたら]き始[はじ]めた。
examples.en: Like a fish back in water, he began working with real energy.

examples.jp: 彼女[かのじょ]は何事[なにごと]もなかったかのごとく、笑顔[えがお]で現[あらわ]れた。
examples.en: She appeared with a smile, as if nothing had happened.

points.notes: Match the form to what follows: noun → {ごとき}, verb/adjective → {ごとく}, end of sentence → {ごとし}.

quiz.q: 彼[かれ]は風[かぜ]の＿＿速[はや]さで走[はし]り去[さ]った。
quiz.en: He ran off with the speed of the wind.

quiz.q: 歳月[さいげつ]は矢[や]の＿＿過[す]ぎ去[さ]っていった。
quiz.en: The years flew by like an arrow.

points.title: 〜まい
points.meaning: (1) will not (firm resolution); (2) probably not
points.structure: Verb (dictionary form) + まい (Group 2: ない-stem + まい also OK; する → するまい／すまい; 来[く]る → 来[く]るまい／来[こ]まい)
points.explanation:
{まい} is the negative counterpart of the volitional {〜よう}. It has two meanings:

**1. Negative resolution (first person):** 'I will never...' — {あんな店[みせ]には二度[にど]と行[い]くまい} 'I'll never go to that shop again'. Often with {二度[にど]と} or {決[けっ]して}.

**2. Negative guess:** 'probably not' = {〜ないだろう}. {嘘[うそ]ではあるまい} 'it's probably not a lie'. The phrase {〜のではあるまいか} 'might it not be that...' is a common soft claim in essays.

**Register:** written and somewhat literary; meaning 1 also appears in determined speech or inner monologue. You already know it from {〜ようが〜まいが} (Unit 13) and {〜ではあるまいし}.

examples.jp: あんな店[みせ]には二度[にど]と行[い]くまい。
examples.en: I'll never go to that shop again.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]の言[い]うことだから、嘘[うそ]ではあるまい。
examples.en: Coming from him, it's probably not a lie.

examples.jp: この雨[あめ]では、明日[あした]の試合[しあい]は行[おこな]われまい。
examples.en: With this rain, tomorrow's match probably won't go ahead.

examples.jp: 少子化[しょうしか]の本当[ほんとう]の原因[げんいん]は、経済的[けいざいてき]な不安[ふあん]にあるのではあるまいか。
examples.en: Might the real cause of the falling birth rate not lie in economic insecurity?

points.notes: In conversation, use {〜ないつもりだ／絶対[ぜったい]〜ない} for meaning 1 and {〜ないだろう} for meaning 2.

quiz.q: もう二度[にど]と同[おな]じ失敗[しっぱい]はする＿＿と心[こころ]に決[き]めた。
quiz.en: I made up my mind never to make the same mistake again.

quiz.q: 彼[かれ]ほどの実力者[じつりょくしゃ]なら、この程度[ていど]の試験[しけん]に落[お]ちることはある＿＿。
quiz.en: Someone as capable as him is unlikely to fail an exam at this level.

points.title: 〜んとする
points.meaning: to be about to; to try to; to intend to
points.structure: Verb ない-stem + んとする (する → せんとする)
points.explanation:
{〜んとする} is the classical version of {〜ようとする}: 'to be on the point of X' or 'to try / intend to X'. The {ん} is the old volitional — the same one in {んがため} and {んばかり}.

Typical uses: {日[ひ]が沈[しず]まんとする頃[ころ]} 'just as the sun was about to set', {新[あたら]しい時代[じだい]が始[はじ]まらんとしている} 'a new era is about to begin'.

One very common expression even in everyday Japanese: {言[い]わんとすること} 'what (someone) is trying to say' — {彼[かれ]の言[い]わんとすることは分[わ]かる} 'I see what he's getting at'. It's also a classic exam question: {筆者[ひっしゃ]の言[い]わんとすることは何[なに]か} 'What is the author trying to say?'

**Register:** literary, except for {言[い]わんとすること}.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]が何[なに]を言[い]わんとしているのか、私[わたし]には分[わ]からなかった。
examples.en: I couldn't tell what he was trying to say.

examples.jp: 日[ひ]が沈[しず]まんとする頃[ころ]、ようやく山頂[さんちょう]にたどり着[つ]いた。
examples.en: Just as the sun was about to set, we finally reached the summit.

examples.jp: 今[いま]まさに新[あたら]しい時代[じだい]が始[はじ]まらんとしている。
examples.en: A new era is about to begin at this very moment.

examples.jp: 作者[さくしゃ]がこの作品[さくひん]で伝[つた]えんとしたのは、平和[へいわ]の尊[とうと]さである。
examples.en: What the author sought to convey in this work is the preciousness of peace.

points.notes: {ん} + {がため} (purpose), {ん} + {ばかり} (almost), {ん} + {とする} (about to) — once you recognise this {ん}, all three become easier.

quiz.q: 筆者[ひっしゃ]がこの文章[ぶんしょう]で言[い]わ＿＿ことは何[なに]か。
quiz.en: What is the author trying to say in this passage?

quiz.q: 長[なが]い冬[ふゆ]が終[お]わり、まさに春[はる]が訪[おとず]れ＿＿としていた。
quiz.en: The long winter was over, and spring was just about to arrive.

units.title: Advanced keigo for business and formal letters
units.summary: The top tier of polite Japanese that you'll need when working in Japan: {申[もう]し上[あ]げる}, {存[ぞん]じる}, {賜[たまわ]る}, the {拝[はい]〜} verbs, {におかれましては}, polite email requests, the right and wrong uses of {させていただく}, and set phrases for formal letters.

points.title: お／ご〜申[もう]し上[あ]げる
points.meaning: (I) humbly do (for you) — the most formal humble form
points.structure: お + Verb ます-stem + 申[もう]し上[あ]げる / ご + する-noun + 申[もう]し上[あ]げる
points.explanation:
You know the humble pattern {お〜する} and {ご〜いたす}. {お〜申[もう]し上[あ]げる} is one step higher: the most formal way to describe your own action directed at someone you respect. It is used for the 'big' speech acts of business and ceremony — apologising, thanking, requesting, reporting, congratulating.

Fixed expressions you'll use constantly:
- {心[こころ]よりお詫[わ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます} — I sincerely apologise
- {よろしくお願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます} — I humbly ask for your kind consideration
- {厚[あつ]く御礼[おんれい]申[もう]し上[あ]げます} — I express my deep thanks
- {お待[ま]ち申[もう]し上[あ]げております} — we look forward to your visit

**Register:** formal emails, letters, speeches, press conferences and announcements. Overkill for everyday office chat with colleagues.

examples.jp: 今後[こんご]ともよろしくお願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We look forward to your continued support.

examples.jp: 調査[ちょうさ]の結果[けっか]をご報告[ほうこく]申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: I would like to report the results of the investigation.

examples.jp: 心[こころ]よりお詫[わ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We offer our sincerest apologies.

examples.jp: 皆様[みなさま]のご来場[らいじょう]を心[こころ]よりお待[ま]ち申[もう]し上[あ]げております。
examples.en: We sincerely look forward to welcoming you all.

points.notes: {申[もう]し上[あ]げる} on its own is the humble form of {言[い]う} ({一言[ひとこと]申[もう]し上[あ]げます} 'allow me to say a few words'). Don't use it for actions that don't involve the other person: {✕お散歩[さんぽ]申[もう]し上[あ]げる}.

quiz.q: このたびはご迷惑[めいわく]をおかけし、深[ふか]くお詫[わ]び＿＿。
quiz.en: We deeply apologise for the inconvenience caused on this occasion.

quiz.q: 皆様[みなさま]のご参加[さんか]を心[こころ]よりお待[ま]ち＿＿おります。
quiz.en: We sincerely look forward to your participation.

points.title: 存[ぞん]じる／存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げる
points.meaning: (humble) to think; to know (a thing / a person)
points.structure: 〜と存[ぞん]じます (think) / 存[ぞん]じております (know a fact) / 存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げております (know a person) / Verb ます-stem + たく存[ぞん]じます (wish to)
points.explanation:
{存[ぞん]じる} is the humble verb for both {思[おも]う} 'think' and {知[し]る} 'know'.

- **Think:** {〜と存[ぞん]じます} — a very polite 'I believe'. Also {恐縮[きょうしゅく]に存[ぞん]じます} (I'm very sorry / obliged), {幸[さいわ]いに存[ぞん]じます}.
- **Know a fact:** {存[ぞん]じております} / {存[ぞん]じません} — the polite way to say 'I know / I don't know'. {存[ぞん]じません} is far more polite than {知[し]りません}.
- **Know a person:** {存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げております} — used when the person known is someone you respect: {お名前[なまえ]はかねがね存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げております} 'I've heard a great deal about you'.
- **Wish:** {〜たく存[ぞん]じます} — very formal 'I would like to'.

Don't confuse with {ご存[ぞん]じ} — the **honorific** for the *other person's* knowing: {ご存[ぞん]じですか} 'do you know?'.

**Register:** business and formal speech; essential in customer-facing jobs.

examples.jp: 申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません、その件[けん]については存[ぞん]じません。
examples.en: I'm terribly sorry, but I don't know about that matter.

examples.jp: お名前[なまえ]はかねがね存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げております。
examples.en: I have heard a great deal about you.

examples.jp: ご多忙[たぼう]のところ恐縮[きょうしゅく]に存[ぞん]じますが、ご確認[かくにん]をお願[ねが]いいたします。
examples.en: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're so busy, but I'd be grateful if you could check this.

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]お目[め]にかかりたく存[ぞん]じます。
examples.en: I would very much like to meet you in person.

points.notes: Common learner mistake: asking a client {✕存[ぞん]じていますか}. Use {ご存[ぞん]じですか} for others and {存[ぞん]じております} for yourself.

quiz.q: 田中[たなか]先生[せんせい]のことは、学生[がくせい]時代[じだい]から存[ぞん]じ＿＿おります。
quiz.en: I have known Professor Tanaka since my student days.

quiz.q: 近[ちか]いうちに一度[いちど]ご挨拶[あいさつ]に伺[うかが]いたく＿＿。
quiz.en: I would like to come and pay my respects in person soon.

points.title: 〜を賜[たまわ]る
points.meaning: to (humbly) receive (favour, support, words) from a superior
points.structure: Noun (ご支援[しえん]・ご愛顧[あいこ] etc.) + を賜[たまわ]る / を賜[たまわ]りますよう(お願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます)
points.explanation:
{賜[たまわ]る} is an extremely respectful verb meaning 'to receive something from someone above you' (like {いただく}, but even more formal). It appears constantly in business letters, emails, speeches and company announcements, almost always with abstract nouns:

- {ご愛顧[あいこ]を賜[たまわ]り} — (thank you for) your patronage
- {ご高配[こうはい]を賜[たまわ]り} — (thank you for) your kind consideration
- {ご指導[しどう]ご鞭撻[べんたつ]を賜[たまわ]りますよう} — (please continue to give) guidance and encouragement
- {温[あたた]かいお言葉[ことば]を賜[たまわ]り} — (thank you for) your kind words

{〜を賜[たまわ]りますよう、お願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます} is the standard super-polite way to close a request.

**Register:** written business and ceremonial language. You'll read it far more than you say it — but you will need to write it.

examples.jp: 平素[へいそ]は格別[かくべつ]のご愛顧[あいこ]を賜[たまわ]り、誠[まこと]にありがとうございます。
examples.en: Thank you very much for your continued patronage.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]より貴重[きちょう]なご意見[いけん]を賜[たまわ]りました。
examples.en: We received valuable feedback from the president.

examples.jp: 皆様[みなさま]から温[あたた]かいお言葉[ことば]を賜[たまわ]り、心[こころ]より感謝[かんしゃ]申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: I am deeply grateful for the kind words I have received from you all.

examples.jp: 今後[こんご]とも変[か]わらぬご支援[しえん]を賜[たまわ]りますよう、お願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We humbly ask for your continued support.

points.notes: {平素[へいそ]は〜を賜[たまわ]り、〜} ('We are always grateful for your...') is the classic first line of a Japanese business email to clients.

quiz.q: 平素[へいそ]より格別[かくべつ]のお引[ひ]き立[た]てを＿＿、厚[あつ]く御礼[おんれい]申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
quiz.en: We are deeply grateful for your continued special patronage.

quiz.q: 引[ひ]き続[つづ]きご指導[しどう]を賜[たまわ]ります＿＿、よろしくお願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
quiz.en: We humbly ask that you continue to give us your guidance.

points.title: 拝[はい]〜する (拝見[はいけん]・拝読[はいどく]・拝聴[はいちょう]…)
points.meaning: humble verbs: (respectfully) see, read, listen, receive, borrow, infer
points.structure: 拝[はい] + Sino-Japanese noun + する／いたす
points.explanation:
{拝[はい]} means 'to bow, to worship'. Prefixed to certain verbs, it makes a humble form for actions directed at something belonging to a respected person:

- {拝見[はいけん]する} — to see / look at (your documents, your work)
- {拝読[はいどく]する} — to read (your letter, your book)
- {拝聴[はいちょう]する} — to listen to (your talk)
- {拝受[はいじゅ]する} — to receive (your email, your document) — business email staple
- {拝借[はいしゃく]する} — to borrow (your pen, your wisdom)
- {拝察[はいさつ]する} — to infer, to imagine (your feelings)

**Register:** {拝見[はいけん]} is everyday business keigo; the others are more formal and mostly written. In an email, {メールを拝受[はいじゅ]いたしました} is a crisp way to acknowledge receipt.

examples.jp: 資料[しりょう]を拝見[はいけん]しました。
examples.en: I have looked at the materials.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]のご著書[ちょしょ]を拝読[はいどく]いたしました。
examples.en: I have read your book, Professor.

examples.jp: メールを拝受[はいじゅ]いたしました。
examples.en: I have received your email.

examples.jp: 少々[しょうしょう]お知恵[ちえ]を拝借[はいしゃく]できますでしょうか。
examples.en: Might I borrow a little of your wisdom?

examples.jp: ご心労[しんろう]のほど拝察[はいさつ]いたします。
examples.en: I can only imagine how worried you must be.

points.notes: {拝見[はいけん]させていただきます} is extremely common but technically double humble; many style guides prefer {拝見[はいけん]します／いたします}. You will hear both.

quiz.q: 先生[せんせい]の論文[ろんぶん]を＿＿いたしました。大変[たいへん]勉強[べんきょう]になりました。
quiz.en: I read your paper, Professor. I learned a great deal from it.

quiz.q: 昨日[さくじつ]の部長[ぶちょう]のご講演[こうえん]を＿＿し、大変[たいへん]感銘[かんめい]を受[う]けました。
quiz.en: I listened to your lecture yesterday and was deeply impressed.

points.title: 〜におかれましては
points.meaning: (as for) you / your company (highly respectful topic marker)
points.structure: Noun (person / organisation addressed) + におかれましては
points.explanation:
{〜におかれましては} is an ultra-respectful replacement for {〜は} when the topic is the respected person or organisation you are addressing. It mostly introduces wishes about their health or prosperity:

{皆様[みなさま]におかれましては、ますますご清栄[せいえい]のこととお慶[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます} 'I trust that you are all in good health and prospering.'

Typical subjects: {皆様[みなさま]}, {貴社[きしゃ]} (your company, written), {先生[せんせい]}, {〇〇様[さま]}.

**Register:** formal letters, speeches and ceremonial greetings. Not for the speaker's own side, and not for everyday emails between colleagues. It's often overused in TV and politics; use it only in genuinely formal contexts.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]におかれましては、お元気[げんき]でお過[す]ごしのことと存[ぞん]じます。
examples.en: I trust you are keeping well, Professor.

examples.jp: 皆様[みなさま]におかれましては、ますますご清栄[せいえい]のこととお慶[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: I trust that you are all in good health and prospering.

examples.jp: 貴社[きしゃ]におかれましては、益々[ますます]ご発展[はってん]のこととお喜[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We are delighted to know that your company continues to flourish.

examples.jp: 寒[さむ]さ厳[きび]しき折[おり]、皆様[みなさま]におかれましては、くれぐれもご自愛[じあい]ください。
examples.en: As the cold is severe at this time of year, please take good care of yourselves.

points.notes: Notice {厳[きび]しき} in the last example — the classical adjective ending {〜き} (= {厳[きび]しい}) survives in seasonal letter greetings.

quiz.q: 貴社[きしゃ]＿＿、ますますご清栄[せいえい]のこととお喜[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
quiz.en: We are delighted to know that your company continues to prosper.

quiz.q: 先生[せんせい]におかれ＿＿、お変[か]わりなくお過[す]ごしのことと存[ぞん]じます。
quiz.en: I trust that you are keeping well as always, Professor.

points.title: 〜いただけますと幸[さいわ]いです／幸甚[こうじん]に存[ぞん]じます
points.meaning: I would be grateful if you could ... (polite written request)
points.structure: ご／お + Verb + いただけますと／いただけましたら／いただければ + 幸[さいわ]いです／幸甚[こうじん]に存[ぞん]じます
points.explanation:
In Japanese business emails, direct requests ({〜てください}) can feel pushy. The standard polite alternative is: 'If you could do X, I would be happy' — {〜いただけますと幸[さいわ]いです}.

Levels of formality:
- {〜いただけると助[たす]かります} — polite but friendly (colleagues)
- {〜いただけますと幸[さいわ]いです} — standard business email
- {〜いただけましたら幸甚[こうじん]に存[ぞん]じます} — very formal ({幸甚[こうじん]} = 'the greatest happiness')
- {〜くださいますよう、お願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます} — formal written request

Often preceded by cushion words: {お手数[てすう]ですが} (sorry for the trouble), {恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが}, {ご多忙[たぼう]のところ恐縮[きょうしゅく]ですが}.

**Register:** written business Japanese. You'll write {幸[さいわ]いです} almost daily if you work in a Japanese office.

examples.jp: お手数[てすう]ですが、ご確認[かくにん]いただけますと幸[さいわ]いです。
examples.en: Sorry for the trouble, but I'd be grateful if you could check this.

examples.jp: ご不明[ふめい]な点[てん]がございましたら、お気軽[きがる]にお問[と]い合[あ]わせいただければ幸[さいわ]いです。
examples.en: If you have any questions, please feel free to contact us.

examples.jp: ご検討[けんとう]いただけましたら幸甚[こうじん]に存[ぞん]じます。
examples.en: I would be most grateful if you would consider this.

examples.jp: 何卒[なにとぞ]ご理解[りかい]くださいますよう、お願[ねが]い申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We humbly ask for your understanding.

points.notes: Read {幸[さいわ]い} here, not {しあわせ}. {幸[しあわ]せです} in an email request would sound oddly emotional.

quiz.q: お忙[いそが]しいところ恐縮[きょうしゅく]ですが、ご返信[へんしん]いただけますと＿＿です。
quiz.en: I'm sorry to bother you when you're busy, but I'd be grateful for a reply.

quiz.q: ご検討[けんとう]いただけましたら＿＿に存[ぞん]じます。
quiz.en: I would be most grateful if you would consider this.

points.title: 〜させていただく (correct use and overuse)
points.meaning: (with your permission) I will humbly do ...
points.structure: Verb causative て-form (させて) + いただく / いただきます
points.explanation:
{〜させていただく} literally means 'I receive (your) letting me do X'. Its core use is when you act **with the other person's permission or for their benefit**, and you want to show gratitude for that:

- Asking permission: {休[やす]ませていただけないでしょうか} 'Might I take the day off?'
- Announcing an action on behalf of others: {会議[かいぎ]を始[はじ]めさせていただきます} 'Let us begin the meeting.'
- Shop/business notices: {休業[きゅうぎょう]させていただきます} 'We will be closed (we ask your understanding)'.

**Overuse:** It has spread into situations where no permission is involved, such as {お送[おく]りさせていただきます} for simply sending something, or {拝見[はいけん]させていただきます} (double humble). These are extremely common, but many Japanese people find heavy overuse grating. When no permission is involved, prefer {〜いたします}: {お送[おく]りいたします}.

**Register:** standard business keigo — use it, but use it deliberately.

examples.jp: それでは、会議[かいぎ]を始[はじ]めさせていただきます。
examples.en: Well then, let us begin the meeting.

examples.jp: 本日[ほんじつ]は体調[たいちょう]不良[ふりょう]のため、休[やす]ませていただけないでしょうか。
examples.en: I'm unwell today; might I take the day off?

examples.jp: 誠[まこと]に勝手[かって]ながら、八月[はちがつ]十三日[じゅうさんにち]から十六日[じゅうろくにち]まで休業[きゅうぎょう]させていただきます。
examples.en: We apologise for any inconvenience, but we will be closed from August 13 to 16.

examples.jp: 先日[せんじつ]はご自宅[じたく]にお招[まね]きいただき、楽[たの]しい時間[じかん]を過[す]ごさせていただきました。
examples.en: Thank you for inviting me to your home the other day; I had a wonderful time.

points.notes: Group 1 verbs take {〜せていただく} ({休[やす]ませて}, {読[よ]ませて}); a common error is the extra {さ}: {✕読[よ]まさせていただく} ('sa-insertion'), which many people consider incorrect.

quiz.q: 恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが、こちらの資料[しりょう]をコピー＿＿いただいてもよろしいでしょうか。
quiz.en: Excuse me, but may I make a copy of this document?

quiz.q: 誠[まこと]に勝手[かって]ながら、年末[ねんまつ]年始[ねんし]は休業[きゅうぎょう]＿＿いただきます。
quiz.en: We apologise for any inconvenience, but we will be closed over the New Year holidays.

points.title: 拝啓[はいけい]〜敬具[けいぐ] (formal letter framework)
points.meaning: set openings and closings for formal letters and emails
points.structure: 拝啓[はいけい] + seasonal greeting + 平素[へいそ]は〜 ... 末筆[まっぴつ]ながら〜 + 敬具[けいぐ]
points.explanation:
Formal Japanese letters (and very formal emails) follow a fixed framework, and each piece is its own little grammar of set phrases:

- **Opening word:** {拝啓[はいけい]} ('respectfully'), closed with {敬具[けいぐ]}. More formal: {謹啓[きんけい]} ... {謹白[きんぱく]}. Informal/urgent: {前略[ぜんりゃく]} ('omitting preliminaries') ... {草々[そうそう]}.
- **Seasonal/health greeting:** {時下[じか]ますますご清栄[せいえい]のこととお慶[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます} (all-season, for companies).
- **Thanks for ongoing relationship:** {平素[へいそ]は格別[かくべつ]のご高配[こうはい]を賜[たまわ]り、厚[あつ]く御礼[おんれい]申[もう]し上[あ]げます}.
- **Closing wish:** {末筆[まっぴつ]ながら} ('last but not least') + wishes for health or prosperity.
- **Closing formula:** {まずは略儀[りゃくぎ]ながら書中[しょちゅう]にてご挨拶[あいさつ]申[もう]し上[あ]げます}.

**Register:** paper letters, formal notices and some corporate emails. Everyday business emails usually skip {拝啓[はいけい]} and start with {いつもお世話[せわ]になっております}.

examples.jp: 拝啓[はいけい]　時下[じか]ますますご清栄[せいえい]のこととお慶[よろこ]び申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: Dear Sir/Madam, I trust this letter finds you in good health and prosperity.

examples.jp: 平素[へいそ]は格別[かくべつ]のご高配[こうはい]を賜[たまわ]り、厚[あつ]く御礼[おんれい]申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: We are deeply grateful for your continued kind support.

examples.jp: 末筆[まっぴつ]ながら、皆様[みなさま]のますますのご健勝[けんしょう]をお祈[いの]り申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
examples.en: Finally, I wish you all continued good health.

examples.jp: まずは略儀[りゃくぎ]ながら書中[しょちゅう]にてご挨拶[あいさつ]申[もう]し上[あ]げます。　敬具[けいぐ]
examples.en: Please accept this letter as my greeting, informal though it may be. Yours sincerely.

points.notes: Pairs must match: {拝啓[はいけい]}→{敬具[けいぐ]}, {謹啓[きんけい]}→{謹白[きんぱく]}／{敬白[けいはく]}, {前略[ぜんりゃく]}→{草々[そうそう]}. Mixing them is a classic mistake.

quiz.q: 手紙[てがみ]を「拝啓[はいけい]」で始[はじ]めたら、「＿＿」で結[むす]ぶ。
quiz.en: If you begin a letter with 'Haikei', you close it with ___.

quiz.q: ＿＿ながら、貴社[きしゃ]のますますのご発展[はってん]をお祈[いの]り申[もう]し上[あ]げます。
quiz.en: Finally, we wish your company continued prosperity.
